articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Karnataka needs a coherent policy on urban mobility

While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 24 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 4 Min Read

📰 Fatal disagreement: on the COP31 summit

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

Developed nations must bear much of the cost of carbon emissions

COP31 ended in Antalya, Türkiye, with a whimper. The 190-odd countries that had convened for nearly 12 days — a close to 50-hour overshoot — failed to agree on an overarching political statement , called a cover text, that acts as a stepping stone to future, collective global action on climate change. Usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations ; the COP31 leadership, helmed by Türkiye and Australia, thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings. The headline sought was a global electrification target: 35% of global final energy consumption will come from electricity by 2035, in the hope that this would reduce direct fossil fuel emissions. Ultimately, the cover text failed to pass muster because the European Union objected to the text’s lack of any explicit mention of ‘fossil fuel,’ let alone its phase-out. The COP process is arduously protracted as even a single country’s objection can stall progress. Country-blocks outside the EU, such as coalitions of the least developed countries, island nations, some South American countries — reportedly 130 countries — were also insistent on fossil fuel language. While COP 31 made some progress on old pathways, such as the Just Transition agreement, it is perplexing that the delegations could not make progress on the other big prong of negotiations: climate finance.

The increase in solar panel installations and the significant shift towards battery use in grid storage and transport did not come cheap: the cost of the land required for their installation, their intermittent nature of being dependent on weather, grid upgrades all carry costs. It is global markets, imperfectly connected, but connected, that have managed to bring it to this stage over decades. India and China, major fossil emitters, with large, still indigent populations, are also leaders in total clean energy installations. Therefore it stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming. Economic crises are a feature, and not a bug, of the interconnected financial system enveloping the world and there are, undeniably, challenges to diverting the necessary finance towards countries most vulnerable to climate change impact. However, it is no longer prudent to sweep this under the rug by scuttling experimental approaches — namely carbon capture — as inimical to the broader commitment to eschew fossil fuel. When the primary framework climate agreement was crafted three decades ago, nobody envisaged AI and the drain that data centres portended or the wars that would see the vociferous antagonists of coal immediately shore up their gas reserves. Without honest good-faith dialogue, the COP is at risk of being a sideshow: a mortal blow to multilateralism.

articles.title: Just verdict: on Myanmar and the International Court of Justice
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Rohingya cannot return unless Myanmar turns democratic

On November 19, the International Court of Justice held that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. It is for the first time that the court has found any state responsible for the crime. The verdict, with nine votes to six, was not lightly reached. Genocide requires proof of an intent to destroy a group. In the absence of direct evidence of a plan, the court could infer that intent only if it was “the only reasonable inference” from the facts, a high bar to affix responsibility. The facts it accepted are harrowing. In 2017, in what Myanmar’s army called “clearance operations” against the insurgent Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, at least 10,000 Rohingya were killed, 1,834 raped and 392 villages destroyed in northern Rakhine State. Over 7,00,000 fled to Bangladesh. Then Army chief Min Aung Hlaing, now Myanmar’s “civilian” President, called the “Bengali problem” an “unfinished job”. Myanmar argued that it had only been fighting insurgents or at worst, driving the Rohingya out or punishing them. The court said that the army drew no distinction between fighters and civilians, had no plan to move anyone, fired on fleeing people and killed children on a scale that could not be explained as punishment. Seen alongside decades of discrimination, the evidence pointed to an intent to destroy.

The incidents of 2017 were no aberration. The army drove lakhs of Rohingya into Bangladesh in 1978 and 1991-92. The junta stripped the Rohingya of citizenship in 1982 and the state branded them as “foreigners” in Arakan, disenfranchising them in 2015. While the junta’s Bamar-Buddhist vision has oppressed every minority, the Rohingya have been subjected to the most brutality. More than 1.2 million are in Bangladesh, living in dilapidated conditions, made worse due to diminished international aid. The court ordered Myanmar to allow their safe, voluntary and dignified return and to compensate them, but it has no means of enforcing its judgment. Only the UN Security Council can, but it will be subject to vetoes by Myanmar’s backers, China and Russia. On the very day of the verdict, the two joined the U.S. in Shenzhen to declare the “immunities of State officials” of “paramount importance”. Others, India among them, have courted the regime in Naypyitaw regardless, following sham elections that made the junta leader civilian President earlier this year. And Rakhine State, mired in civil war, is now mostly held by the Arakan Army which is accused of atrocities against the Rohingya. Only a truly democratic, federal, plural and peaceful Myanmar can bring the Rohingya home in safety.

articles.title: Core accountability: On core sector performance
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Even a low base effect could not push India’s oil and gas sectors into growth

The core sector performance in October is a good example of how statistical distortions can create incorrect assessments of the economy. The 10.9% growth rate, a series high, has been celebrated as a sign of the Indian economy’s strength and resilience. There is, no doubt, an aspect of this has been reflected in the numbers, especially to do with infrastructure creation. However, the much more impactful factor behind the high core sector growth was a low base effect. The overall Index of Core Industries grew just 0.8% in October 2025 and so, in relation, the performance in October 2026 looked that much faster. This low base effect is even starker when looking at individual sectors within the index. The coal sector grew at a blistering 23% in October, more than twice its growth rate in the previous month. Yet, a large part of this was propelled by the fact that the sector had contracted nearly 8.5% last October. The rest of the sector’s growth was driven by demand of the electricity and iron ore sectors, or so the data show. The electricity sector also grew at a series high of nearly 22% in October, but on the back of a near-7% contraction in October last year. This base effect anomaly is likely down to the fact that the festive season starts at different but similar points every year. As such, a more accurate reading of the economy will be possible once the data for November are available.

The construction-related sectors seem to have seen genuine growth, a reflection of the government’s ongoing infrastructure push. The iron ore sector’s growth rate accelerated to a three-month high of 26.4% in October 2026 as compared to a growth of 8.7% in the same month last year. Steel grew at 7.3% versus 9.5% last year, and cement by 15.4% versus 5.2%. articles.title: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Climate action has to be timely, with adequate resources and monitoring

That all was not well with the Green India Mission was clear even before its approval. After the UPA-I government announced it in 2008, the Ministry of Rural Development had objected to its financial design much before the Union Cabinet approved it in 2014. But the Environment Ministry proceeded anyway and retained largely the same arrangement when it revised the Mission in 2021. Following the Comptroller and Auditor General’s report, on November 19, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) upbraided the Ministry for the Mission’s virtual failure and for still not having issued the implementation guidelines for the revised form. The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.

Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.
Editorial Context: Paper tiger: On the Green India Mission. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

The original 10-year vision was to expand forest and tree cover by 5 million hectares (mha), improve forest quality on another 5 mha, improve forest-related livelihoods for 3 million households, and sequester up to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. The outlay was ₹46,000 crore. In 2014, the Cabinet approved ₹13,000 crore for 1.4 mha each of the first two objectives by 2018, but to be supported to the tune of 81.5% by Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA), National Afforestation Programme (NAP), and MGNREGS funds. In 2021-22, the Ministry folded the NAP into the Mission and, in mid-2025, unveiled a revised version with an allocation of ₹12,190 crore to improve forest cover on 25 mha by 2030, including 24 mha through other schemes. The government had thus expanded the primary target but left the Mission responsible for only 1 mha.
• Together with the CAMPA, NAP, and MGNREGS funds never materialising, it is no surprise that the programmes to improve forest quality and forest cover have respectively fallen short by 91.8% and 97.5% vis-à-vis the 2014 target. The Environment Ministry had assembled a large programme around resources that it knew it could not control. Pro-climate work in practice ought to span government schemes to deliver action and justice, and the Ministry ought to have formalised the division of responsibilities and accounting system. The PAC’s new demand that the Ministry submit an implementation timetable is insufficient. From the Jal Shakti Abhiyan in 2019 to the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan in 2024, the government has often floated new programmes banking significantly on funds from existing schemes — an untenable policy when the latter also have their own obligations. And if the VB-G RAM G scheme was to also advance climate justice, the government should not have undermined the erstwhile demand-driven funding model and shifted more financial responsibility to the States. Climate action has to be timely, for which the Union government must dedicate adequate resources and proactively ensure that its initiatives are implemented.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Indian CIE industry is the world’s third-largest, with a market size of ₹97,000 crore in FY 2024-25, yet about 45% of it depends on imports, says Minister
The Union Cabinet on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) approved a ₹11,000-crore scheme to boost the country's Construction and Infrastructure Equipment (CIE) manufacturing ecosystem.

Addressing the media after the Cabinet meeting, Information and Broadcasting Minister (I&B) Ashwini Vaishnaw said the scheme will run for eight years, starting in FY2026-27, and aims to build indigenous capacity in advanced CIE and position India as a key player in the global market.
The Indian CIE industry is the world's third-largest, with a market size of ₹97,000 crore in FY 2024-25, yet about 45% of it depends on imports, the Minister said.

The scheme includes a two-year gestation period (FY2026-27 to FY2027-28) to set up manufacturing facilities, followed by a five-year incentive disbursement period (FY2028-29 to FY2032-33) and a final year (FY2033-34) to settle incentives for incremental sales made in FY2032-33.

According to an official statement, driven by accelerated growth in infrastructure (roads and ports) and housing, the industry is projected to increase more than double, reaching a market size of around ₹2,28,100 crore by FY2029-30.

The scheme covers seven categories of equipment that are fully or largely imported, including tunnel boring machines, off-highway trucks, excavators, cranes, loaders, piling rigs, and drilling machines. The scheme also provides for establishing a State-of-the-art, dedicated CIE testing facility in the country.
Last month, China announced new export controls on key machinery, including tunnel boring machines, in a move that could adversely impact India's infrastructure development.

According to the statement, the scheme, to be implemented by the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI), aims to incentivise domestic manufacturing of CIE and its components and to establish a dedicated CIE testing facility in the country, thereby enhancing self-reliance and positioning India as a key player in the Global CIE market.

The scheme has two components: a sales-linked incentive and a grant for a CIE testing facility. Under the sales-linked incentive, incentives will be provided on the incremental sales value of eligible CIE equipment and components to approved applicants across two categories — eligible OEMs and Component Manufacturers.

Graded Incentive rates range from 13% to 8% of incremental sales value over five years. Under the grant for a CIE testing facility — a grant of up to ₹375 crore, like Viability Gap Funding — will be given for setting up a dedicated CIE testing facility.

articles.title: YSRCP demands apology over demolition of Anjaneya Swamy temple in Tirupati district for NH expansion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The road alignment could have been changed to save the temple, say YSRCP leaders Velampalli Srinivas and Malladi Vishnu

The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) leaders Velampalli Srinivas and Malladi Vishnu have demanded a public apology from the Chandrababu Naidu government and the Endowments Department over the demolition of the centuries-old Abhaya Anjaneya Swamy temple at Anjaneyapuram, Tirupati district, for National Highway expansion.

Addressing a press conference on Wednesday, they alleged that the demolition using bulldozers and earthmovers had hurt Hindu sentiments and amounted to an attack on religious traditions. They questioned why rituals such as Dhyana Adhivasam and Jala Adhivasam, which they said were prescribed under Agama traditions before removing a temple, were not performed.

సనాతన ధర్మం గురించి మాట్లాడే పవన్ కళ్యాణ్‌కు.. దేవాలయాలను కూల్చుతుంటే సనాతన ధర్మం గుర్తురావడం లేదా? పక్క రాష్ట్రంలోని ఆంజనేయస్వామి గుడికి డబ్బులు ఇచ్చానని చెప్పుకునే నువ్వు.. నీ రాష్ట్రంలో ఆంజనేయ స్వామి గుడిని బుల్డోజర్లతో నిర్దాక్షిణ్యంగా కూలుస్తుంటే కనీసం మాట్లాడవా? దేవాలయాలను కూల్చే ప్రభుత్వం కూటమి ప్రభుత్వమని అందరూ తెలుసుకోవాలి. -వెల్లంపల్లి శ్రీనివాస్ గారు, మాజీ మంత్రి #SaveTemplesFromTDP

The leaders argued that the road alignment could have been changed instead of demolishing the historic temple. They pointed out that the government had diverted a road to facilitate a hospital and questioned why a similar option was not considered in this case.

They accused the Endowments Department of failing to protect temples and demanded that the Minister and officials explain their response to the incident. Referring to incidents at temples in Tirupati, Srikalahasti, Srisailam, Simhachalam and Kashibugga, they alleged that the government had failed to ensure the safety of devotees and the protection of temple property and cattle.

Contrasting the present government with the previous YSRCP regime, they said the Srivani Trust had supported the construction of thousands of temples, while the Dhupa Deepa Naivedyam scheme had extended assistance to priests.

రాష్ట్రంలో కూటమి ప్రభుత్వం వచ్చినప్పటి నుండి జేసీబీల ప్రభావం ఎక్కువగా కనిపిస్తోంది. గతంలో టీడీపీ ప్రభుత్వంలో 2014-19లో జేసీబీలు కనిపిస్తే పేద, మధ్య తరగతి వాళ్ళకి ఇబ్బంది ఉండేది. కానీ.. 2024-2026లో జేసీబీలు చూసి దేవాలయాలు కూడా భయపడే దుస్థితి. నిన్న తిరుపతి దగ్గర వందల సంవత్సరాల చరిత్ర ఉన్న అభయాంజనేయ స్వామి గుడిని నిదర్శనంగా కూల్చేయడమే నిదర్శనం. -వెల్లంపల్లి శ్రీనివాస్ గారు, మాజీ మంత్రి #SaveTemplesFromTDP
They also recalled the demolition of temples during the Krishna Pushkarams in Vijayawada under the previous Chandrababu Naidu government, claiming that the YSRCP regime had rebuilt some of them.

Referring to an incident at a Venkateswara Swamy temple in Eluru, they alleged that a trust board member entered the temple wearing footwear and assaulted a priest. They also claimed that pressure was exerted to settle the matter without filing a police complaint.
Questioning the silence of Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan and BJP leaders over the temple demolition, they said coalition partners who spoke about Sanatana Dharma should also take responsibility.

articles.title: AIMIM MLA Akhtarul Iman sparks row with sexist remarks on Muslim women
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: I ask you to refrain from attending weddings where you cannot even differentiate whether a person is Jamila or Sita, he said
All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul-Muslimeen (AIMIM) Bihar president and MLA Akhtarul Iman triggered a controversy after a video of him making sexist remarks went viral on Tuesday (November 24, 2026).

“Even a tawaif (courtesan) does not sit as decked out and adorned as the bride. Have you no shame, groom? And you, the groom’s father — have you no shame either? Other people are staring at your daughter-in-law; don’t you have any shame? This is the characteristic behaviour of a pig, who invites another male to join him with his female,” said the MLA, who represents the Amour constituency, in the video.

Mr. Iman made the remarks at a religious gathering in Saharsa on Monday (November 23, 2026). He also questioned traditions within the Muslim community, such as muh-dikhai (the ritual of unveiling the bride’s face), the acceptance of gifts during walima (wedding receptions), and excessive spending.

“On one hand, a daughter wears a burqa after marriage, yet on the other, 16-year-old girls walk around with their hair wide open. I ask you to refrain from attending weddings where you cannot even differentiate whether a person is Jamila or Sita,” he said.
The AIMIM MLA said while the number of people in society wearing the topi (skullcap) has increased, the dupatta (headscarf) has slipped not only from daughters’ heads but also from their chests.

He added that someone is often tasked with sitting down with pen and paper to record money received from guests, describing this as social posturing and an unnecessary tradition, and urged people to rethink these practices.

The Bihar State Commission for Women took suo motu cognisance of the matter and served him a show-cause notice asking for a reply within a week. Commission member Sajal Jha said he has no right to dictate what women should or should not do, adding that his language is insulting to all women, irrespective of caste or religion.
Bihar BJP media coordinator Danish Iqbal strongly opposed the AIMIM MLA’s statement, saying such remarks cannot be tolerated in India.
“Those who wish to adopt Sharia in place of the Constitution have the option to go to countries like Afghanistan or Pakistan; they are free to leave India and move there,” Mr. Iqbal said.

When The Hindu asked him about his derogatory remarks, Mr. Iman said he had not insulted anyone and had only blamed the groom and the father-in-law, adding that people were making an issue out of nothing.

articles.title: Over 23 lakh vehicles in Keralam have failed to clear Pollution Under Control checks since 2021
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Motor Vehicles department in coordination with State Police has imposed a total penalty of ₹43.2 crore from 2022 to September 30, 2026 for violations related to pollution-control requirements
About 23.9 lakh vehicles in Keralam have failed the mandatory Pollution Under Control (PUC) testing over the past five years.

A total of about 5.74 crore PUC tests were held from the financial year 2021 to September 30, 2026. About 5.5 crore vehicles had passed the test while 23.9 lakh vehicles failed to clear it, according to estimates by the Department of Transport.

About 57.5 lakh tests were conducted from March 2026 to September 30, 2026 and 1.87 lakh vehicles failed the PUC test during this period, said a report furnished by the Transport department before the National Green Tribunal in a case related to a plea for reducing vehicular emissions and promoting environmentally sustainable transport systems in the State.
CAQM report in Supreme Court shows huge gap between policy and groundwork in curbing vehicular emissions

Officials of the Transport department said that vehicles failing the PUC test were required to rectify the defects and undergo retesting before being given permission to resume operations. The pollution monitoring has been strengthened through a network of PUC testing centres that are integrated with the Vahan/Parivahan portal. The department has introduced an Aaadhaar-based mobile OTP system to prevent and reduce fake applications for getting the Pollution Under Control certificate, they said.

The Motor Vehicles department in coordination with the State Police had imposed a total penalty of ₹43.2 crore from the year 2022 to September 30, 2026 for violations related to pollution-control requirements, including vehicles without valid PUC certificates and those with high-emissions. Of the total penalty of ₹43.2 crore slapped, the authorities have collected ₹11.96 crore as on September 2026, according to official estimates.

Health experts have sounded caution against the threats caused by vehicular pollution. “Diesel smoke has been classified as carcinogenic to humans (Group 1) by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), which means that exposure at heavy doses over a long period carries a risk of cancer,” pointed out Rajeev Jayadevan, convener of the research cell of the Indian Medical Association, Kerala.
Supreme Court moots allowing only BS-VI-compliant vehicles into Delhi

“Children risk stunting, people with respiratory diseases suffer worsening symptoms, and pregnant women who breathe this air are at higher risk of delivering preterm babies. Air pollution also increases the burden of non-communicable diseases, linked with heart attacks, strokes, high blood pressure, and diabetes,” Dr. Jayadevan said.

articles.title: The Hindu’s coffee table book on exploration of the Western Ghats released
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The book titled, ‘Mountains of Our Destiny: The Western Ghats, A Journey Through The Southern Monsoon Mountains by Vrinda Ramanan and J. Ramanan is a sequel to ‘Mountains of our Destiny: An Expedition to the Indian Himalaya’, also by the same authors.

The Hindu launched a coffee table book titled, ‘Mountains of Our Destiny: The Western Ghats, A Journey Through The Southern Monsoon Mountains’, on Wednesday (November 25, 2026). Authored by Vrinda Ramanan and J. Ramanan, mountaineers, writers and photographers, the book was launched by Tamil Nadu Forests Minister R.V. Ranjith Kumar. The first copies were received by Rohit Ramesh, Director, Suresh Nambath, Editor, and L.V. Navaneeth, CEO, The Hindu . The book is a sequel to ‘Mountains of our Destiny: An Expedition to the Indian Himalaya’, also by the same authors.

Speaking on the occasion, the Minister noted the importance of the forests, rivers and mountains to sustaining agriculture, livelihoods and ecological balance. He highlighted the need to ensure forest conservation, spoke of the measures taken by the government to improve upon work being done, such as AI technology to prevent elephant deaths on railway tracks and in the control of forest fires, and congratulated the authors on their work.

Author J. Ramanan explained that the two mountain ranges: the Himalayas and the Western Ghats formed the bedrock of India’s existence. Without them, he said, we would not have had our rivers. The 1,500 km Western Ghats in particular, recognised as a biodiversity hotspot, was one of the richest ecological resources in the country, sustaining thousands of lives. The monsoon in India, Mr. Ramanan said, is shaped by the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. The book was an attempt to create awareness about, and educate people on the importance of maintaining ecological balance through their preservation.

Through more than 400 photographs, field experiences and narratives, the book explores the geology, wildlife, plants, indigenous communities and the intricate web of life that sustains these mountains. It also examines the growing pressures of plantations, invasive species, tourism, dams and other human interventions, highlighting the urgent need for conservation.

The book is available at The Hindu ’s online bookstore: https://publications.thehindugroup.com/ . The cover price of the book is ₹2,999. At present, the book is available at a special launch offer price of ₹2,249 for a limited period of time. Those interested can also scan the QR code to buy a copy.

articles.title: J&K clerics apologise, offer ‘repentance prayers’ for standing during Vande Mataram at Waqf Board function
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: After Vande Mataram was played at the first Waqf Day function, clerics say they recited the ‘kalima’ in repentance; Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulama may seek legal opinion

A group of prominent Muslim clerics who attended the Waqf Day function in Srinagar on Monday (November 23, 2026) apologised on Wednesday and “offered repentance prayers” over standing during the Vande Mataram song, as the incident triggered a wave of protests from religious groups in J&K, including the Muttahida Majlis-e-Ulama (MMU).

The controversy was sparked by the November 23 event of the J&K Waqf Board that was attended by Union Minority Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology, Srinagar. At the first-ever Waqf Day function organised by BJP leader and J&K Waqf Board chairperson Darakhshan Andrabi, the full Vande Mataram song was played with several top Muslim clerics on the dais as well as in the audience. National Conference (NC) MP Mian Altaf Larvi and Shia cleric and J&K Peoples Conference leader Imran Reza Ansari also attended the function.

Facing criticism, Maulana Farooq, accompanied by other clerics, said in an online video, “Some things unacceptable from the Sharia point of view took place on the occasion. We repent for the same. We went outside the venue, immediately recited ‘ kalima ’ in a congregation and offered our repentance. Ulemas from other sects also attended it. We did not recite anything from our hearts. Allah will accept our repentance.”

Those who attended the function included Mufti Syed Basharat, Mufti Farooq, Mufti Inayatullah Qasmi, Maulana Farooq, Maulana Basharat Sakafi, Pir Syed Ejaz, Maulana Zakir, Abdul Rashid Dawoodi and imams of the Dastigeer Sahib shrine and the Hazratbal shrine.

Maulana Rahmatullah, who heads Kashmir’s biggest seminary, Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, welcomed the “act of repentance by the Muslim priests for their mistake”. “I congratulate these religious leaders for their immediate repentance prayers and reciting the ‘kalima’ again for the mistake. Allah must be pleased with them.”

Mr. Rahmatullah said anything that interferes with the faith of Muslims “is not acceptable”. “Mr. Dawoodi should have mentioned the Supreme Court ruling and clarified that the Vande Mataram cannot be forced. It was not a political stage but a Waqf function. I had advised Ms. Andrabi beforehand that you belong to a family who have spread Islam. I fail to understand why she committed this wrong. She should have conveyed to sing Jana Gana Mana but not play with religious sentiments and sing Vande Mataram . I ask Mr. Dawoodi to educate Ms. Andrabi on this, but then granting ‘ imaan ’ is in the hands of Allah,” said Mr. Rahmatullah.

Meanwhile, the MMU, an amalgam of religious organisations headed by Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, said, “It has categorically made clear on several occasions in the past, the fundamental and non-negotiable principle of Tawheed in Islam — the absolute Oneness of Allah. Islam strictly prohibits associating any partner with Allah or attributing divinity to any person, object, land or creation.”

The MMU said it was highly “regrettable and unacceptable” that Vande Mataram was played at the function of the Waqf Board, an institution entrusted with safeguarding Muslim religious endowments and their sanctity. “There was no legal obligation to play Vande Mataram simply because it was an official function, and playing it was optional,” said the MMU.
It said the Waqf Board went ahead “with utter disregard for the fundamental religious beliefs and sensitivities of Kashmiri Muslims, which has caused deep hurt and anguish among people.”

“The MMU expresses grave concern over the increasingly routine inclusion of Vande Mataram at official government functions across Muslim-majority Jammu and Kashmir, despite the well-known religious reservations of Muslims. Such imposition disregards their religious convictions and constitutional rights and deepens distrust and alienation,” said the MMU spokesman.

Islam strictly prohibits associating any partner with Allah or attributing divinity to any person, object, land or creation.”

The MMU said it was highly “regrettable and unacceptable” that Vande Mataram was played at the function of the Waqf Board, an institution entrusted with safeguarding Muslim religious endowments and their sanctity. “There was no legal obligation to play Vande Mataram simply because it was an official function, and playing it was optional,” said the MMU.

It said the Waqf Board went ahead “with utter disregard for the fundamental religious beliefs and sensitivities of Kashmiri Muslims, which has caused deep hurt and anguish among people.”

“The MMU expresses grave concern over the increasingly routine inclusion of Vande Mataram at official government functions across Muslim-majority Jammu and Kashmir, despite the well-known religious reservations of Muslims. Such imposition disregards their religious convictions and constitutional rights and deepens distrust and alienation,” said the MMU spokesman.

articles.title: Global climate talks must shut door on fossil fuel ‘clout’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The breakdown in the Antalya summit has deepened the crisis of confidence in climate diplomacy, making transparency and accountability in the negotiating process more urgent than ever.

The failure of the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, to agree on its central political statement, with countries unable to bridge their differences over fossil fuels and other key questions of climate action, has exposed the fragility of international climate cooperation. It should also sharpen scrutiny of who gets access to climate negotiations, whose interests they represent and what safeguards keep decisions accountable to the public.

The Türkiye summit ended without agreement on an overarching statement. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

The breakdown does not show that fossil fuel lobbying caused the impasse. But it does make more urgent a separate question about the credibility of the process. A forum that asks governments to make decisions in the global public interest must be transparent about who is seeking to shape those decisions, what interests they represent and how conflicts are managed.

The international climate negotiations that take place every year still lack a comprehensive, enforceable system to identify and manage conflicts of interest involving powerful commercial interests, including fossil fuel companies and state-owned energy businesses. The Antalya conference has underlined why that gap matters.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he shared the “deep disappointment” of many that the conference was unable to reach consensus on a statement that typically sends a policy signal to all nations. Some separate negotiating decisions were reached though. Nevertheless, the absence of a political consensus was a serious setback.

articles.title: Oil and gas production to pick up in 4-5 years as recent measures take effect, Petroleum Ministry says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: In a note accessed by The Hindu, the Ministry has said that the oil and gas industry has a long gestation period and so exploration and finance decisions taken more than a decade ago are affecting the industry now

The government expects domestic oil and gas production to pick up in the next 4-5 years as several steps taken in the recent past begin to bear fruit in an industry typically characterised by long gestation periods, The Hindu has learnt.
According to an analysis by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the current contraction in domestic oil and gas production is due to factors that took place more than a decade ago.

However, since then, the government has taken steps such as increasing drilling and exploration to record levels, changing laws and rules to provide stable terms to explorers, and opening new avenues for exploration.

“The steps taken in the last few years — new acreage, record drilling, deepwater wells and the revival of Mumbai High — will start showing up in production over the next three to four years,” the note asserted. “That is the nature of this sector: the decisions of one decade decide the output of the next.”
The note also argues that now, unlike earlier, the profits of oil and gas companies upstream companies like ONGC and Oil India are being used to fund exploration rather than subsidies.
“Until 2015, ONGC and Oil India were made to fund a large share of the subsidy on diesel, LPG and kerosene, through discounts on the crude they sold to oil marketing companies,” the note said.

According to data with the Ministry, ONGC paid ₹49,421 crore towards this subsidy in 2012-13 against a profit of ₹20,926 crore, and in 2013-14 paid ₹56,384 crore towards this subsidy against a net profit of ₹22,095 crore.

“In both years ONGC gave away more than twice what it earned,” the note said. “Money that should have gone into finding new oil and gas went into keeping retail prices down. This burden was ended from 2015-16. ONGC now keeps its earnings and has sharply raised its spending on exploration.”
According to the latest data on the Index of Core Industries, the oil and gas sectors have contracted continuously for 22 and 28 months, respectively.

“In this sector it takes five to ten years to go from awarding a block to first production,” a note prepared by the Ministry and accessed by The Hindu said. “Output in 2026 is the result of what was, and was not, done a decade ago.

articles.title: SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank retain D-SIB status; RBI maintains capital requirements
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The additional capital requirements are intended to enhance the resilience of these institutions.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has retained State Bank of India (SBI), HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank in its 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), maintaining their respective positions under the same bucketing structure as in 2025.

Under the RBI’s framework, SBI, placed in Bucket 4, will have to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital requirement of 0.80% of its Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs). HDFC Bank, classified under Bucket 2, will have an additional CET1 requirement of 0.40%, while ICICI Bank, placed in Bucket 1, will have to maintain 0.20%.
These additional capital requirements are over and above the Capital Conservation Buffer, strengthening the banks’ ability to absorb financial shocks and contain systemic risks.

The latest classification is based on data collected from banks as of March 31, 2026. Under the D-SIB framework, banks are categorised into different buckets according to their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs), with higher scores attracting higher additional capital requirements.

The RBI introduced the Framework for Dealing with D-SIBs on July 22, 2014, subsequently updating it on December 28, 2023. The framework requires the central bank to publicly disclose the names of designated D-SIBs annually, beginning in 2015, and assign them to appropriate buckets based on their systemic importance.

SBI and ICICI Bank were initially designated as D-SIBs in 2015 and 2016, respectively. HDFC Bank joined the list in 2017, when all three banks were identified as systemically important financial institutions.

📈 Economic, Banking & Finance 📅 23 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 2 Min Read

📰 SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank retain D-SIB status; RBI maintains capital requirements

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

The additional capital requirements are intended to enhance the resilience of these institutions.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has retained State Bank of India (SBI), HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank in its 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs), maintaining their respective positions under the same bucketing structure as in 2025.

Under the RBI’s framework, SBI, placed in Bucket 4, will have to maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital requirement of 0.80% of its Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs). HDFC Bank, classified under Bucket 2, will have an additional CET1 requirement of 0.40%, while ICICI Bank, placed in Bucket 1, will have to maintain 0.20%.

These additional capital requirements are over and above the Capital Conservation Buffer, strengthening the banks’ ability to absorb financial shocks and contain systemic risks.

The latest classification is based on data collected from banks as of March 31, 2026. Under the D-SIB framework, banks are categorised into different buckets according to their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs), with higher scores attracting higher additional capital requirements.

The RBI introduced the Framework for Dealing with D-SIBs on July 22, 2014, subsequently updating it on December 28, 2023. The framework requires the central bank to publicly disclose the names of designated D-SIBs annually, beginning in 2015, and assign them to appropriate buckets based on their systemic importance.

SBI and ICICI Bank were initially designated as D-SIBs in 2015 and 2016, respectively. HDFC Bank joined the list in 2017, when all three banks were identified as systemically important financial institutions.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Rampur Bushahr’s Lavi Fair in Himachal Pradesh traces a Himalayan journey from wool and barter to women entrepreneurs and digital payments

What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

articles.title: UK police charge two men over a break-in at Prince William and Princess Catherine’s country home
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II
Two men have been charged with burglary at the country home of Prince William and Princess Catherine, police said on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

The Norfolk Police force says Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. They are due in court later on Wednesday.

Police officers were called on Monday evening to reported “suspicious activity” at an address on the royal family's rural Sandringham estate in eastern England. After a search involving police dogs, drones and a helicopter, two men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespassing.
William and Kate’s Kensington Palace office declined to comment on security matters.
Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom house on the Sandringham estate, was a wedding present to the couple from the late Queen Elizabeth II.

William and Kate use the secluded red brick Georgian mansion about 110 miles (171 kilometres) north of London as a country residence on weekends. The couple and their three children spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, west of London, which they have described as their “forever home.”
Intruders have breached royal properties several times over the years.

In October 2024, burglars broke into the Windsor Castle estate west of London and stole a pickup truck and a quad bike from a farm building. Charles and Queen Camilla weren’t at Windsor Castle at the time, but it was reported that William and Kate were in their nearby house.

Three years earlier, a man armed with a crossbow was detained on the castle grounds. Jaswant Singh Chail was later sentenced to nine years in prison after admitting he had been encouraged by a chatbot to kill Elizabeth.

In 1982, intruder Michael Fagan managed to sneak into the queen’s private chambers while she was in bed. The queen spent 10 minutes chatting with the burglar before raising the alarm when he asked for a cigarette.

articles.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang says he is in therapy as comeback rally fades
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Jensen Huang told staff it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because U.S. President Donald Trump had pressured the board

Jensen Huang apologised to Nvidia staff and said he was in therapy on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), as a stock rally triggered by his shock return as CEO faltered amid persistent doubts over the probes he faces and the fate of the AI investment boom.

"I made some terrible mistakes," Mr. Huang told an hourlong all-hands meeting at the company's Santa Clara, California, headquarters, The New York Times reported after reviewing a livestream of the event.
He told staff it was "not acceptable" that he had broken a code of conduct he had helped write, and dismissed suggestions that he was back because U.S. President Donald Trump had pressured the board.
But Mr. Trump told CNBC on Monday (November 23, 2026) that he had been in contact with directors about Mr. Huang's return. "I spoke to them, let me put it that way," he said. "And I convinced them."
After vaulting more than 30% on Monday (November 23, 2026), Nvidia shares were down about six percent at close on Tuesday (November 24, 2026).
"The optimism faded quickly" for Nvidia, wrote Fawad Razaqzada of Forex.com, with "questions over corporate governance and board oversight still lingering."
So far Monday's surge was a "one day wonder...We are not seeing an upside follow through today at all," said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.

Mr. Huang resigned on November 12 over extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, a departure that sent shares in Nvidia and companies closely linked to the AI buildout tumbling.
Mr. Trump was reportedly talked into backing the return of the Taiwan-born CEO after top tech investors told him the U.S. economy and Wall Street depended on it.
Nvidia said Monday (November 23, 2026) that it had reinstated Mr. Huang as chief executive after receiving information from the US government that he did not pose a national security risk.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to ​overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering ‌systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters.

The November 12-13 outage ​hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms ⁠and disrupted airline communications, fueling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents.
Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO ‌Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption.

The Code Red signified the most severe and urgent alert to address weaknesses in Microsoft’s engineering and operational practices after the outage disrupted ‌Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and ‌other ⁠Microsoft 365 products.
It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, ⁠M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday.
Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” drive to ​overhaul how it prevents and responds to major service failures after a 24-hour outage exposed shortcomings in its engineering ‌systems and crisis response, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters.

The November 12-13 outage ​hit governments from Australia and Japan to the United States, delayed trading firms ⁠and disrupted airline communications, fueling broader concerns about the vulnerability of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft blamed the outage on an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July. CEO ‌Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption.

It was the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, ⁠M365 Core President Jason Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday.

Never before had so many customers been without email for so long, he said. “Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Henderson added.

articles.title: At least two Indians among 11 injured in Houthi attack in Riyadh; New Delhi condemns strike
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence said a tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District came under what it described as a "terrorist attack" by Houthi militia
Two Indians were among those injured in an attack on a financial district in Riyadh that triggered strong condemnation from New Delhi.
India also denounced continued strikes targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.

“Two Indians are among those injured in the attack on Riyadh financial district. The embassy of India in Riyadh is providing all possible assistance to the injured and their families,” the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said.
The attack was carried out on Tuesday (November 24, 2026). Local authorities said the injured included two Saudi citizens, three Nepalese and four Egyptian nationals.

The MEA said India strongly condemns the attack in Riyadh as well as the continued strikes targeting civilian, economic and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. “These attacks seriously endanger civilian lives, violate the sovereignty of Saudi Arabia, and undermine regional security and stability. We call for immediate cessation of such attacks,” it said in a statement.

India also reiterated its firm solidarity with the people and government of Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed its unwavering support to the Kingdom in safeguarding its sovereignty and territorial integrity.
“We earnestly hope that peace and normalcy will return to the region at the earliest,” the MEA said.
There has been a sudden escalation in tensions in West Asia, especially after the Houthis carried out several strikes on Saudi Arabia.
The West Asia conflict began in February following attacks on Iran by the U.S. and Israel. New Delhi has consistently called for finding a solution to the conflict through dialogue and diplomacy.

India has been specifically voicing serious concern over the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s civilian infrastructure and economic assets, cautioning that such strikes undermine regional stability and threaten freedom of navigation through the Bab-el-Mandeb strait.

articles.title: WHO chief calls on U.S. to lift oil blockade on Cuba, citing health impact
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: United Nations has also repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, calling the U.S. fuel blockade a violation of international ‌law and the human rights of all ​Cubans

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called on Tuesday (November 24, 2026) for the ​immediate lifting of the U.S. fuel blockade on Cuba, ‌warning that the measure was putting the lives ​of children at risk.

“The intensification of ⁠fuel restrictions and sanctions is causing direct harm to the Cuban people, especially the most vulnerable,” Mr. Tedros said on ‌a recent visit to Cuba that included tours of several healthcare facilities in ‌Havana.
“It is endangering their lives, including the ‌lives ⁠of children.”

During his three-day visit, the official ⁠said his organization would contribute $2 million to help strengthen Cuba’s national immunization program and provide essential medical equipment to healthcare facilities.

Like ​the World Health Organization, ‌the United Nations has also repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, calling the U.S. fuel blockade a violation of international ‌law and the human rights of all ​Cubans.

The Cuban government says U.S. sanctions have led to daily power outages lasting ⁠20 hours or more, critical shortages of medicines and surgical supplies, and a decline in health indicators, such ‌as infant mortality rates.
Washington argues the energy blockade is intended to push for political change on the island, and says that exports of food and medicine are subject to legal exemptions.

Tensions between the two nations have soared since the ‌administration of U.S. President Donald Trump ramped up pressure on ​Cuba since January, imposing a fuel blockade on the island and stiff sanctions ⁠against a swath of Cuban officials and state entities.
An annual ⁠non-binding resolution calling for an end to a U.S. embargo on the island ‌has passed in favor of Cuba in the UN General Assembly by wide margins every ​year since 1992.

articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The Little Stint travels thousands of kilometres between its Arctic breeding grounds and Indian wetlands. But as shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands

The little stint, a 25-gram shorebird, comes in lakhs from the Arctic to the shores of India, particularly to Point Calimere. “It’s an unforgettable sight,” says S Sivakumar, who has been involved in monitoring shorebirds in the Gulf of Mannar for over a decade. The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May. “In the 1980s, the little stint could be seen in several lakhs at any point of time. Even now, the numbers are still over a lakh as the Point Calimere Wetland Complex covers over 300 kilometres across coastal Tamil Nadu ,” says Sivakumar, assistant director at the Bombay Natural History Society’s Bird Migration Study Centre at Point Calimere, adding that such long-term observations help scientists understand how bird populations and their habitats are changing.
The birds remain through the winter months and depart between March and April, sometimes later in May | Photo Credit: S Sivakumar

The tiny bird’s annual migration journey, a feat of endurance, involves multiple stopovers across different landscapes, each of which must provide sufficient food and safe resting grounds. As shrinking mudflats and changing landscapes threaten its feeding and resting habitats, this tiny shorebird tells an important story about conserving wetlands.

Ashvin Viswanathan, scientist at Bird Count India , places the little stints as the most visible representatives of a special group of shorebirds that breed in the Arctic. “ This group is declining rapidly due to climate change and loss of habitat. Little stints too are declining in India according to SoIB,” he says, referring to the State of India’s Birds assessment. Their widespread presence, he adds, indicates the health of wetland ecosystems in India as well as conditions in the Arctic. The fact that the little stint is still a fairly common bird does not mean that it is beyond risk. It’s numbers and distribution can help draw attention to changes taking place across the habitats it depends on.
The numbers are still over a lakh at Point Calimere wetlands | Photo Credit: S Sivakumar

The bird’s preparation for migration is as fascinating as the journey itself. “Before setting off, they enter a phase of intense feeding called hyperphagia. They feed voraciously to build up fat reserves that act as fuel during its journey.

This can add 50 to 75 percent to the bird’s body weight. There are also physiological changes, some organs shrink in size as the bird prepares for the demands of sustained flight,” explains Sivakumar adding that India is an important destination along the Central Asian Flyway that connects the bird with wintering habitats further South. The birds can be found along several coastal wetlands, including Point Calimere, Pulicat, parts of Puducherry and Kanyakumari, the Sundarbans, and the mudflats of Gujarat and Maharashtra. Across Tamil Nadu, the species is familiar to birders. “You can spot them at wetlands such as Kurichi and Ukkadam in Coimbatore,” says birder K Selvaganesh adding that the flock plays an important part of the food chain as prey for raptors, including the Western marsh marrier and the brahminy kite.

Goa-based Rakesh Dhareshwar, a wildlife photographer says Goa and the wider west coast are reliable places to find them each season. “This year, I was delighted to see them inland too, at Bhigwan in Maharashtra, during a mid-Novemeber trip. However, shorebirds worldwide are in decline. Loss of coastal and inland wetlands, reclamation of mudflats, and pollution threaten stopover and wintering sites these birds depend on. The good news is that we can fix this. Protecting wetlands, salt pans and estuaries, and sharing spaces thoughtfully with people can make a real difference.”
Shorebirds worldwide are in decline | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

In his new book, Little Stint: A Migrant’s Tale (Neythal Pathipakam), author Byju H explores the bird’s remarkable journey through a blend of science and unconventional storytelling allowing the bird to narrate its own life, beginning with emerging from an egg in the Arctic tundra. “I wanted readers to travel with the bird,” he says adding that the book also highlights the fact that the bird’s ability to navigate vast distances depends on the availability of suitable wetlands along its migratory route.

articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The November full moon, known as the Beaver Moon, appears larger and brighter than usual due to its proximity to Earth

Skywatchers were treated to a dazzling view as the Beaver Supermoon lit up the night skies on Tuesday (November 24, 2026). The November full moon, known as the Beaver Moon, appears larger and brighter than usual due to its proximity to Earth. Here is more about the celestial display and when you can watch the next supermoon

The moon revolves around the Earth in an oval-shaped path (elliptical orbit). A supermoon occurs when the moon rises near perigee (the point in its orbit closest to earth), appearing larger and brighter than usual. This year’s full moon (November 24) is known as the Beaver Supermoon because this is when beavers prepare for the winter and also the time of year to set beaver traps before the swamps and rivers froze.

Supermoon appears 14 per cent bigger and 30 per cent brighter than a micromoon, which occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being near its apogee — the farthest point from Earth in its orbit.
The “Beaver moon” is a moniker for November’s full moon adopted by the Old Farmer’s Almanac , supposedly from Algonquian languages once spoken by Native Americans in the New England territory.

Though not a rare occurrence, supermoons only happen three to four times a year and always appear consecutively. Because the Moon is in its closest point to Earth, it can cause higher tides than usual, according to NASA.
Supermoon is visible to the naked eye wherever skies are clear and no special equipment is required.
The next supermoon will be on December 24, 2026. The last supermoon of the year, it will be the largest full moon.
The first supermoon of 2027 will be on January 22, also known as the Wolf Supermoon.

‘Wolf moon’ is a traditional name for the first full moon that happens in January. Many full moons have old seasonal names, often popularised in folklore, that helped people keep track of the time of the year before the advent of modern calendars.
Beaver Moon is seen rising in Chandigarh on November 24, 2026. | Photo Credit: SHASHI SHEKHAR KASHYAP

What if the plants choking the forests of the Nilgiris could be given a second life as works of art?An ongoing exhibition in Gudalur hopes to tell that story, bringing together conservation, craftsmanship and narratives of the intimate relationship between people and the natural world. “For all of us, sharing space with wildlife is part of everyday life,” says Rhea Antony, who takes care of storytelling and design at The Elephant People, a social enterprise based in Gudalur in the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve that makes hand-carved wildlife sculptures, masks, and everyday objects from invasive plant species like Lantana camara and Senna spectabilis.
Handcrafted objects made using invasive species vegetation | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

The exhibition is an attempt to draw attention to the changing landscapes of the Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve, where the invasive species have spread across native habitats. The Elephant People collective works with Forest Departments of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka in clearing these invasive species. The exhibition features large-scale sculptures, smaller carved pieces, and interactive storytelling experiences. For children, there will be facilitated painting and story-building workshops, alongside interactive art installations that let them explore the forest through play. These installations offer opportunities to learn about different species, their habitats, and the sounds they make.

fullParagraphs: PCD is a rare genetic disorder that affects the cilia, which help move mucus and other particles out of the respiratory tract. Mucus is therefore not cleared effectively and builds up in the respiratory tract, increasing the risk of recurrent infections

Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) is a rare inherited disorder that affects tiny, hair-like structures in the body called cilia. When these structures fail to move properly, mucus and bacteria accumulate in the airways, increasing the risk of recurrent respiratory infections and long-term lung damage.

While there is currently no cure, early diagnosis and regular treatment can help manage symptoms and preserve lung function. Recent research into the genetic causes of PCD is also offering new insights into the disease and its diagnosis.

articles.title: When public duty meets medical privacy
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A legislator undergoing prolonged treatment may retain the ability to perform official responsibilities. Functional capacity, rather than diagnosis alone, is therefore central to the legal question of what the public has the right to know

articles.title: The cow, the flea and the genome: One Health and the statecraft of prevention
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: A cattle virus at home and a plague scare abroad make the same argument this World One Health Day: life is epidemiologically indivisible, and the institutions that govern and study it must learn to be so too

In the second of his Major Rock Edicts, cut into stone in the third century BCE, Ashoka records that he has provided medical care of two kinds, for people and for animals, and has had healing herbs planted wherever they were lacking. Twenty-three centuries before the phrase existed, an Indian State treated the health of humans, animals and the land as a single charge of government. Rudolf Virchow, who introduced the word ‘zoonosis’, restated the idea for the age of the microscope: between animal and human medicine there is no dividing line, nor should there be.

Modern governance, however, forgot what Ashoka and Virchow knew. It allotted people to one ministry, livestock to another and forests to a third, and pathogens, which recognise no such allocation of business, have exploited the gaps ever since. One Health, which the world marks on November 3, is the effort to recover that lost unity with the tools of the 21st century by bringing human, animal and environmental health into a common framework for research, surveillance and prevention. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , which regards the world as one family, resonates with this understanding of interconnected life.

This year the case makes itself. Lumpy skin disease (LSD) has returned to India. The September forecast from ICAR-National Institute of Veterinary Epidemiology and Disease Informatics’ early-warning system placed 219 districts across 28 states and Union Territories at risk, and Rajasthan had recorded more than 10,400 cases in 10 eastern districts by mid-September. In Siberia, a young technician at Irkutsk’s anti-plague institute died in early October, of what Russian authorities called pneumonia of unknown cause, amid reports of pneumonic plague. Nearly 200 people were placed under observation. Whatever the final diagnosis, Yersinia pestis , the organism of the Black Death, has never left us. It persists in rodents and their fleas, from the marmots of the Central Asian steppe to the prairie dogs of New Mexico and the rats of Madagascar.

Neither story respects a departmental boundary. LSD does not infect people, but it drains milk cans, household incomes and children’s nutrition. Plague is at once a problem of wildlife ecology, laboratory biosafety, clinical medicine and public trust.

articles.title: Spinning wheels: on urban mobility in Karnataka
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Karnataka needs a coherent policy on urban mobility

While Karnataka has spent years disputing motorcycle owners’ right to carry paying passengers, Bengaluru — with the dubious distinction of having one of the world’s highest travel times per unit distance — struggles with inadequate public transport capacity and lacklustre intermediate options. The Supreme Court ruling on November 20 to dismiss Karnataka’s appeal was thus straightforward, allowing motorcycles to be registered as transport vehicles. The State has often called bike taxis unsafe, yet has not improved the prospects of safer options. Earlier this year, the Centre for Science and Environment estimated the number of buses in urban centres nationwide to be 70% short of the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs benchmark and that 400 cities with populations between a lakh and 10 lakh altogether lacked organised bus services. In March, the BMTC reported a fleet of around 7,000 buses in Bengaluru, versus the 13,000 by 2025 envisaged by the Comprehensive Mobility Plan. Expanding the number of Metro stations also creates more demand for travel to and from stations, but the operating costs of the public transport corporation expected to serve that demand are not covered by the resulting increase in rail ridership.

Overall, Karnataka has struggled to set up a consistent transport policy. An expert committee recommended against bike taxis in Bengaluru for first- and last-mile connectivity and in favour of better walking infrastructure and bicycle rentals in 2019, only for the State to launch the electric bike-taxi scheme in 2021, then rescind it in 2024 over safety concerns and drivers’ disputes. The market for short booked journeys is also dysfunctional. But while allowing bike taxis could temper autorickshaw fares, the State must investigate drivers’ operating costs, the difference between the paid and the received amounts, and prevent large platforms from exploiting the market. Finally, while the Union Road Transport Ministry has reported that 46.2% of all road deaths involved two-wheeler users, two-wheelers’ safety relative to autorickshaws and cabs, by the number and distance of journeys, is unclear. The State should require aggregators to report injuries and fatalities and investigate the consequences of drivers’ earnings being linked to the number of trips undertaken. The Union government’s 2025 Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines already address passenger security, fares, and insurance while allowing States to authorise privately registered motorcycles through aggregators. Karnataka should exercise this additional power. A large national programme is required to address funding for public transport, which is necessary even when it is not immediately profitable.

articles.title: Assam CM downplays ‘fight’ between two IPS officers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The confrontation occurred at an Assam Police battalion headquarters in the western part of the State on November 22, 2026
Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma on Tuesday (November 24, 2026) downplayed an alleged clash between two senior Indian Police Service officers at a party as a “personal fight”.

The incident, involving a Deputy Inspector General of Police (DIG) and a Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP), occurred at an Assam Police battalion in the western part of the State on Sunday night (November 22, 2026).

“There was a fight between two persons at a private programme. We have nothing to do here, as it was personal and had no connection with the Police Department. Sometimes, we also end up having arguments,” the Chief Minister told journalists on the sidelines of an official event.
“We would have done something had it happened during official duty. I have no comment on a personal matter,” he said.
According to reports, the DIG in question was among several senior police officers invited to a party the SSP had organised.
The DIG and the SSP allegedly quarrelled during the event. It turned physical, reportedly leaving the SSP injured.
Another senior IPS officer, reportedly assigned by Director General of Police Harmeet Singh, resolved the matter.
The trigger for the fight could not be ascertained. Police did not issue any statement.

articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
